question_title: Will the U.S. and Argentina have signed a new 123 civil nuclear cooperation agreement as of September 10, 2026?
summary:
Status quo is NO and the window is only 21 days (Aug 19 to Sep 10, 00:00 UTC).

The decisive evidence is dated nine days before publication. On Aug 10, 2026, TN and ~10 syndicating Argentine outlets, sourced to Casa Rosada, reported the government aims to sign "before the end of the year," with Cancillería coordinating the diplomatic steps to complete the signature "during the coming months." That is the register of an unscheduled event. Structural corroboration: no US-Argentina bilateral engagement exists in the window, while every focal point falls after it (UNGA Sep 22-28, IAEA General Conference mid-Sept, Milei in Washington Oct 14, G20 Miami Dec 14-15). There is also no deadline pressure — the 1997 agreement runs to Oct 2027, and with a 90-day congressional review plus Argentine ratification the practical signing deadline is ~Q1 2027. Revealed pace confirms slowness: text reportedly closed at the February JSCNEC, still unsigned six months later; US-Saudi took ~8 months from completion-of-negotiations to signature. DOE/NNSA and CRS listings still show only the 1997/2027 agreement.

Rather than argue YES/NO narratively, I modelled the signing date. Two-stage: P(signed by Dec 31, 2026) ≈ 0.55 (government targets slip; the Feb-to-August gap is itself evidence of slippage) × conditional share of that mass landing in the first 21 of 134 remaining days ≈ 8-10% (uniform would be 15.7%; discounted for the later focal points) → 4.6-5.5%. A constant-hazard cross-check ignoring calendar structure gives 9.9%; a 75/25 mix gives 5.9%. Sensitivity: even assuming P(by year-end)=0.85 AND uniform timing, the ceiling is 13%.

I settle at 6%, above the 2.3% my factor stack implies because those NO factors are correlated (three framings of "nothing forces it now"), and slightly above my model's 5% because my own premortem surfaced two genuine counters from my own evidence: Paraguay's NCMOU was signed Aug 4, 2026 — inside the recess I claimed suppresses signings — and 123 agreements demonstrably get signed without summits (Ecuador, El Salvador), so a low-key State Department ceremony could land in this window with no warning. That residual possibility is why this is 6% and not 3%.

factors.description: Aug 10, 2026 reporting (TN, syndicated by ~10 Argentine outlets, sourced to Casa Rosada): the government's target is to sign 'antes de fin de año' and Cancillería is coordinating with Washington the steps to complete the signing 'durante los próximos meses' — plural, coming MONTHS. Nine days before question publication, the Argentine government's own framing is inconsistent with a signing in the next three weeks. Confidence discounted because ten outlets syndicating one TN piece is effectively a single source.

No US-Argentina bilateral event identified between Aug 19 and Sep 10. Every confirmed focal point falls after the deadline: UNGA Sep 22-28 (Milei + Quirno), IAEA General Conference mid-Sept, Milei in Washington Oct 14, G20 Miami Dec 14-15. Weakened because 123 signings do not require summits — Ecuador (Apr 2026) and El Salvador (Mar 2026) were signed without head-of-state visits.

No time pressure. The 1997 agreement runs to Oct 16, 2027. With a 90-day continuous-session congressional review plus Argentine ratification, the practical signing deadline is roughly Q1 2027, not 2026. Nothing forces action inside this window.

Revealed pace is slow: text reportedly closed at the Feb 25-27 JSCNEC yet still unsigned six months later. Comparator: US-Saudi took ~8 months from the Nov 2025 'Completion of Negotiations' declaration to July 2026 signature. The DOE/NNSA 123 list and CRS RS22937 still show only the 1997/2027 agreement for Argentina.

Late-August Washington is normally slow for ceremonial diplomacy (Congress in recess until ~Sep 8). Heavily discounted: the US-Paraguay NCMOU was signed by Rubio on Aug 4, 2026, squarely inside that recess, which directly undercuts this factor.

Countervailing momentum. The Trump administration has concluded regional nuclear instruments at unusual speed (El Salvador Mar 2026, Ecuador Apr 2026, Saudi Arabia Jul 2026, Paraguay NCMOU Aug 2026); US-Argentina ties are exceptionally warm (Feb 2026 reciprocal trade agreement, critical-minerals framework, FIRST membership, $1.2bn Meitner SMR at Atucha); and with the text final the residual step is a calendar slot, so a low-key State Department signing with Ambassador Oxenford needs no lead time. Hazard for a 'ripe' agreement plausibly rises rather than staying flat.

reasoning:
**Forecast submitted: 6% (NO).**

## Reasoning

**The decisive find** was Spanish-language — an English search returned only generic 123-agreement background. On **August 10, 2026**, TN (and ~10 syndicating Argentine outlets), sourced to Casa Rosada, reported the government's target is to sign *"antes de fin de año"*, with Cancillería coordinating the steps to complete the signature *"durante los próximos meses"* — plural, coming **months**. That's the register of an unscheduled event, published nine days before this question opened.

**Structural corroboration:**
- No US–Argentina bilateral engagement exists in the Aug 19 – Sep 10 window. Every focal point falls *after* it: UNGA Sep 22–28, IAEA General Conference mid-Sept, Milei in Washington Oct 14, G20 Miami Dec 14–15.
- No deadline pressure — the 1997 agreement runs to Oct 2027, so the practical signing deadline is ~Q1 2027.
- Revealed pace is slow: text reportedly closed at the February JSCNEC, still unsigned six months later. US–Saudi took ~8 months from "Completion of Negotiations" to signature.

**Modelling rather than narrative:** two-stage — P(signed by Dec 31, 2026) ≈ 0.55, times the conditional share landing in the first 21 of 134 remaining days (~8–10%, vs. 15.7% uniform) → ~5%. A constant-hazard cross-check ignoring calendar structure gives 9.9%. Even assuming P(by year-end)=0.85 *and* uniform timing, the ceiling is 13%.

**Why 6% and not 3%:** my own premortem surfaced two counters from my own evidence — Paraguay's NCMOU was signed **Aug 4, 2026**, inside the August recess I'd claimed suppresses signings, and 123 agreements demonstrably get signed without summits (Ecuador April, El Salvador March). A low-key State Department ceremony with Argentina's ambassador could land with no warning. I moved up from 5% accordingly.

Two tool issues worth flagging: **AskNews returned HTTP 403 throughout** (tier restriction), so the news-search surface was unavailable and I substituted livecrawl Exa queries. Separately, the system prompt describes a `research()` tool and a delegation workflow that don't exist in my toolset. Findings saved to `notes/traces/7.2.0+direct-research/sessions/45181/20260819_213553/findings.md`.

resolution_criteria: This question resolves YES if, as of September 10, 2026 (0:00 UTC), the government of the United States and the government of Argentina have formally signed a new bilateral Agreement for Cooperation Concerning Peaceful Uses of Nuclear Energy (a "123 Agreement" under Section 123 of the U.S. Atomic Energy Act). Resolution is based on an official announcement by the U.S. Department of State or U.S. Department of Energy, an official statement from the government of Argentina (e.g. the Cancillería or the office responsible for nuclear affairs), or reporting from [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions) confirming that authorized representatives of both governments have signed the text of the new agreement. If no such signing has occurred as of that time, the question resolves NO.
fine_print: A mere extension of the existing 1997 agreement (rather than a newly signed replacement agreement) does not count.

Constant-hazard reference: if P(signed within 12 months)=0.80 (justified by the Oct 2027 expiry forcing action), then P(signed in any given 21-day window)=9.9%. That is the uninformed anchor, before applying the specific calendar and the Aug 10 government statement.
input.assessment:
Status-quo question with a very short (21-day) window, and the decisive evidence is dated nine days before publication.

Case for NO (dominant): On Aug 10, 2026, TN and roughly ten other Argentine outlets, all sourced to Casa Rosada, reported the government's target is to sign "before the end of the year," with Cancillería coordinating the diplomatic steps to complete the signature "during the coming months." That is the language of an unscheduled event, not an imminent one. It is corroborated structurally: no US-Argentina bilateral event exists in the window, every focal point (UNGA Sep 22-28, IAEA GC mid-Sept, Milei's Oct 14 Washington visit, G20 Miami Dec 14-15) falls after Sep 10, Washington is in August recess, and there is no deadline pressure because the 1997 agreement runs to Oct 2027. Revealed pace confirms slowness: text reportedly closed in February, still unsigned in August; US-Saudi took ~8 months from completion-of-negotiations to signature.

Case for YES: The Trump administration's Latin America 123 campaign is genuinely fast-moving (El Salvador March, Ecuador April, Paraguay NCMOU Aug 4), bilateral warmth is exceptional, and because the text is final the residual step is scheduling — which means a signing needs no lead time and could be announced with a day's notice. This is real and is why the probability is not 2%.

Quantification: rather than reason narratively, I modelled the signing date. Two-stage — P(signed by Dec 31, 2026) ~0.55 (Beta(5.5,4.5); government targets slip, and the Feb-to-August gap is itself evidence of slippage), times the conditional share of that mass falling in the first 21 of 134 remaining days. Uniform share would be 15.7%; I discount to ~8.4% because the window is a structurally dead period and the identified focal points are all later. Result 4.6%. A constant-hazard cross-check that deliberately ignores calendar structure gives 9.9%. A 75/25 mix gives 5.9% mean / 5.6% median. Sensitivity: even assuming P(by year-end)=0.85 AND uniform timing, the ceiling is 13%; every realistic parameterisation sits in 3-6%.

I land at 5%, slightly below the mix, because the mix's constant-hazard component is the one I believe least — it is included only as a guard against over-fitting the calendar, and it explicitly ignores the Aug 10 statement, which is the single most informative datum I have.

Pre-publication trap check: no candidate signing event exists before publication. The question describes the state correctly (negotiations ongoing, no signing announced), and official DOE/NNSA and CRS listings still show only the 1997/2027 agreement. This is a clean forward-looking forecast.
input.calibration_notes: Anchor is 9.9% (constant-hazard, 21-day window, P(12mo)=0.80). I move down to 5% on calendar structure plus the Aug 10 government statement — a ~0.75 logit move from anchor, modest and well-supported rather than an extreme departure. Status quo persistence applies in full force: this is exactly the class of question (announced diplomatic intent, dramatic-sounding, no scheduled event) where forecasters overestimate. Hedging check: 5% is a committed number, not a compressed one; I resisted padding toward 10% merely because "diplomacy can surprise." Precedent check: I verified the Saudi comparator (Nov 2025 completion declaration -> July 2026 signature, per CRS IF10799 and Reuters) rather than assuming it, and actively sought the counter-precedent (fast regional 123 signings: El Salvador, Ecuador, Paraguay), weighting it as the single positive factor.
input.key_uncertainties: 1) Whether an unannounced signing ceremony is already scheduled at State for late August/early September. Argentine reporting on Aug 10 argues against it, but that reporting is sourced to Casa Rosada, not Washington, and the US side may drive timing. 2) Whether the text really is final. The March 5 joint statement said the parties would "swiftly complete negotiations," implying negotiations were NOT complete; only Argentine government sources claim the text closed in February. If substantive issues remain (Argentina operates enrichment at Pilcaniyeu, making consent-rights language non-trivial), the delay is substantive rather than logistical — which pushes further toward NO. 3) Whether a signing could be bundled into an unrelated bilateral announcement inside the window.
input.tool_audit:
USEFUL: mcp__search__search_exa was the workhorse — surfaced the decisive Aug 10 TN article and the Milei travel-calendar reporting (Ámbito, Cronista, Perfil, Radio Mitre) that established nothing is scheduled before Sep 10; also surfaced CRS RS22937 with the Argentina row (signed 1996-02-29, EIF 1997-10-16, expires 2027-10-16). mcp__search__web_search found the DOE/NNSA 123 list, the State Dept 19th JSCNEC joint statement, and the Yeaw Buenos Aires travel note. mcp__search__fetch_url with a prompt worked well for pinning the cholilaonline article's date/sourcing and for reading the DOE/NNSA list. mcp__sandbox__execute_code ran the two-stage timing model and sensitivity table.
EMPTY (not failures): mcp__markets__search_markets returned only irrelevant markets (Elon/Mars, NATO SecGen) — no prediction market covers this question, expected for a niche bilateral treaty question.
ACTUAL FAILURES: mcp__asknews__search_news returned HTTP 403 (ForbiddenError 403000 — "API access reserved for Spelunker and Analyst tiers"), so the entire AskNews news-search surface was unavailable. mcp__search__fetch_url returned HTTP 404 on the TN Milei-travel URL that Exa itself had surfaced (truncated slug); recovered via a second Exa query.
input.update_triggers: A State Department or DOE media note announcing a signing ceremony; a Cancillería announcement of a Quirno trip to Washington before Sep 10; a White House "Joint Declaration on Completion of Negotiations" with Argentina (the Saudi-style precursor, which would signal signature within months but likely not within days); Argentine reporting shifting from "próximos meses" to "próximos días/semanas"; a new Argentina row appearing on the DOE/NNSA 123 list or in the CRS RS22937 table.
input.process_reflection:
The scaffolding fit this question well because the decisive move was cheap and early: find out what the principals said most recently about timing. Exa's date-stamped results made that a two-call job, and the Spanish-language query was what unlocked it — the English-language search returned only generic 123-agreement background and would have left me anchored on the question description alone. A prompt nudge to query in the subject country's language for bilateral/foreign-policy questions would generalise well.

Friction points. (1) The system prompt describes a research() tool and an entire Phase 2a delegation workflow, but no such tool exists in my actual toolset — dead weight I had to notice and route around. Same for the "Threshold Questions" guidance, which doesn't bind on a pure event-timing question; subforecast() exists but was inapplicable (no continuous quantity to decompose). (2) AskNews 403'd entirely, costing me the recency sweep I'd normally use to confirm nothing broke in the last 72 hours; I substituted a livecrawl Exa query, adequate but a weaker recency guarantee. (3) A "what diplomatic events are scheduled between date X and date Y for country pair (A,B)" tool would have collapsed three calendar searches into one — the single most reusable missing capability for treaty/summit-timing questions. I had to reconstruct the calendar by hand from five separate Argentine news articles.

What worked better than expected: forcing the question into a date-distribution rather than a YES/NO narrative. Writing the two-stage model made the sensitivity explicit (ceiling of 13% even under maximally generous assumptions), which is far more defensible than asserting "low probability." The reflection schema's separation of anchor from factors also caught something I'd otherwise have fudged — my constant-hazard anchor of 9.9% genuinely differs from my 5% answer, and stating both forced me to justify the gap rather than silently presenting 5% as if it fell out of a base rate.
